title: Smart power grid
like: a power company reading millions of smart meters
brief: A power company has 5 million smart meters. Each reports usage every 15 minutes, and they all try on the quarter hour. Customers see their usage, billing needs exact totals for seven years, and a regulator checks that records are kept safely. Control commands to home batteries and thermostats must never run twice.

clarify.q: Can a meter reading be lost?
clarify.a: No. Readings are the basis of every bill. A meter keeps its readings and resends, so the same reading may arrive twice.
Seven years for billing. The last 30 days must be fast to query; older data can be slow and cheap.
When power returns, thousands of meters report at once. A short link failure between the substations and the cloud must not lose data.
That every action is logged, data is encrypted with managed keys, backups exist and old records are kept for the required years.

requirements.users: 5 million meters, 3 million customers who look at usage (approx.)
notes: Each reading is about 100 bytes; estimate long-term storage before adding copies.
5 million meters every 15 minutes is about 5,500 batches a second on average, and the quarter-hour waves are about 25 percent higher (approx.).

Scored data retention: at least 2555 days on active authoritative stores. Copies used only for search or reports can be rebuilt. Local device history and rollup policies still require the separate protocol check.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

text.name: Synchronized rush
text.description: Many callers send requests together instead of spreading them over time.

debrief.headline: A synchronized rush hit {node}.
debrief.fix: Spread scheduled work over time and keep spare capacity on the affected path. A rate limiter protects downstream work by rejecting excess calls, so it cannot by itself meet every availability target.

numbers.label: Meter batches per second at peak
Seven years of readings at about 100 bytes
numbers.how: 480M x 100 B = 48 GB a day, x 365 x 7

hints: Seven years of data is much more than any fast database should hold. How can old data move somewhere cheaper while the last month stays quick?
A stream absorbs the quarter-hour waves, a time-series database keeps 30 days, and a cold archive keeps the rest. Add an audit log, key service and backups for the regulator.

Balancer, event stream (3 brokers), two stream workers, a 3-node time-series database with 30 day retention, a data lake and cold archive for older data, a small API with a cache for the customer portal, an idempotency store for control commands, audit log, key service, backups and alerts.

editorial.summary: A fleet of meters is a metronome: everyone calls on the quarter hour, so the system must take big even waves, never lose a reading and keep it for seven years. Hot, warm and cold storage is the main lever on cost, and the regulator needs proof, not promises.

designs.name: Stream, hot database, cold archive
designs.why: The stream flattens each quarter-hour wave and keeps readings safe if a link drops. Thirty days live in the time-series database for fast queries, and everything older goes to the lake and archive at about a hundredth of the storage price. The audit log, key service and backups answer the regulator.

tradeoffs: Hot storage costs roughly ten to a hundred times more than cold. Keeping only 30 days hot is the largest saving in the design.
Four days of stream retention is enough to survive a weekend of trouble and costs little. One day is not.
Resending readings is safe because a reading has a meter id and a time; the store ignores the second copy.
Text messages cost about a cent each and push alerts cost nothing, so alerts go out by push and only the urgent ones get a text.
The audit log, key service and backups are small monthly costs and each prevents a failed audit check.
editorial.realWorld: Utilities often collect 15-minute interval readings from millions of meters and are required to keep billing records for several years (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Smart power grid: A worker sends a message, then crashes before recording success. What key and delivery states would you store so a retry does not send it twice?
correctness.discussion: Give each logical message a stable key, scoped to its recipient and channel, and enforce a unique constraint on that key. Save the request and an outbox entry in one transaction, then track pending, sending and delivered states. A queue alone does not prevent duplicates. If the provider accepts the send but the worker crashes, retry with the same provider idempotency key or query its status. Without provider support, exactly-once external delivery cannot be guaranteed: discuss whether a possible duplicate or a possible missed message is acceptable.

fields.label: The provider accepts the operation, then the worker crashes before saving success. What state is durable?
options: Unknown outcome, with the original logical operation key
Failed, so the retry gets a new key
fields.explanation: Missing local success does not prove the provider rejected the operation.

fields.label: The queue redelivers that operation. What can establish one external effect?
options: Check a local cache, then send without a provider key
Reuse the provider idempotency key or reconcile its recorded outcome
fields.explanation: A local lookup and a remote side effect are not atomic. Without endpoint support, one external effect cannot be guaranteed; report uncertainty and choose an explicit recovery policy.
